1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Use the vercel-react-view-transitions skill 16 17 The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 18 19 Install the skill: 20 21 ```bash filename="Terminal" 22 npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 23 ``` 24 25 Then give the agent this prompt: 26 27 ```prompt 28 Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 29 ``` 30 31 To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. 32 33 ## Example 34 35 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 36 37 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 38 39 You can find the resources used in this example here: 40 41 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 42 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 43 44 View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. The App Router uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which contain all stable React 19 changes as well as newer features like `ViewTransition`. You do not need to install `react@canary` yourself. 45 46 > [!NOTE] 47 > React's integration uses newer View Transitions API features (transition types and `view-transition-class`), available in Chromium 125+ and recent Safari and Firefox versions. Some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally; the transitions do not animate. 48 49 Import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 50 51 ```tsx 52 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 53 ``` 54 55 `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 56 57 ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 58 59 The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 60 61 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 62 63 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 64 65 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 66 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 67 import Image from 'next/image' 68 import Link from 'next/link' 69 70 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 71 return ( 72
73 {photos.map((photo) => ( 74 75 76 77 78 79 ))} 80
81 ) 82 } 83 ``` 84 85 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 86 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 87 import Image from 'next/image' 88 89 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 90 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 91 92 return ( 93 94
95 96
97 98 ) 99 } 100 ``` 101 102 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 103 104 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 105 106 The morph plays when the destination content renders in the same commit as the navigation, which is the case with prefetched (cached) pages. If the destination suspends into a fallback first, no pair forms, and the content animates with its enter animation instead when it arrives. 107 108 #### Customizing the morph animation 109 110 The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"` together with `default="none"`. The `share` prop assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 111 112 ```tsx 113 114 115 116 ``` 117 118 Add the same props to both Step 1 snippets (`photo-grid.tsx` and `photo-content.tsx`). `default="none"` keeps each named image from running its own crossfade on every unrelated transition. Without it, every named `` animates whenever any transition runs on the page. When you add `default="none"` to a named pair, keep the explicit `share`. With `default="none"` and no `share` prop, the pair silently stops morphing. 119 120 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 121 ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 122 animation-duration: 400ms; 123 } 124 ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 125 animation-name: via-blur; 126 } 127 @keyframes via-blur { 128 30% { 129 filter: blur(3px); 130 } 131 } 132 ``` 133 134 The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 135 136 ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 137 138 The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 139 140 Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 141 142 In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 143 144 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 145 146 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 147 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 148 149 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 150 const { id } = await params 151 152 return ( 153 156 157 158 } 159 > 160 161 162 163 164 ) 165 } 166 ``` 167 168 As in Step 1, `default="none"` prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph. 169 170 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 171 172 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 173 :root { 174 --duration-exit: 150ms; 175 --duration-enter: 210ms; 176 --duration-move: 400ms; 177 } 178 179 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 180 animation: 181 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 182 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 183 } 184 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 185 animation: 186 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 187 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 188 } 189 190 @keyframes fade { 191 from { 192 filter: blur(3px); 193 opacity: 0; 194 } 195 to { 196 filter: blur(0); 197 opacity: 1; 198 } 199 } 200 @keyframes slide-y { 201 from { 202 transform: translateY(10px); 203 } 204 to { 205 transform: translateY(0); 206 } 207 } 208 ``` 209 210 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 211 212 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 213 214 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 215 216 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 217 218 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. 2	
3	You have a dev server that serves HTML to a browser. An agent in a
4	headless container can't open a browser window — so "run the app" means
5	launching the dev server, driving a headless Chromium against it, and
6	producing a screenshot that proves the page rendered.

8	Don't write a browser driver. Use `chromium-cli`.
9	
10	## Dev server
11	
12	Find the dev command (`package.json` `scripts.dev`, `Makefile`,
13	README), start it in the background, and wait for it to actually serve:
14	
15	```bash
16	npm run dev &   # or yarn dev, pnpm dev, make serve, ./dev.sh
17	timeout 30 bash -c 'until curl -sf http://localhost:3000 >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done'
18	```
19	
20	Don't `sleep 5` — poll the port. Stop by killing the port's listener
21	— `lsof -ti:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN | xargs -r kill` — before relaunching,
22	or the next run hits `EADDRINUSE`. (`$!` after `npm run dev &` is only
23	the npm wrapper; npm doesn't forward SIGTERM to the server it spawned,
24	so the port kill is what actually frees it.) Avoid `pkill -f` with a
25	broad pattern — it can match the agent's own command line and kill the
26	session.
27	
28	## Drive
29	
30	`chromium-cli` is a headless-Chromium REPL. Pipe a script to stdin:
31	
32	```bash
33	chromium-cli --session app <<'EOF'
34	nav http://localhost:3000
35	wait-for text=Dashboard
36	screenshot
37	click button:has-text("New item")
38	fill input[name="title"] Smoke test
39	press Enter
40	wait-for text=Smoke test
41	screenshot
42	console --errors
43	EOF
44	```
45	
46	Screenshots land in `chromium_cli/sessions/app/screenshots/` (latest
47	symlinked as `screenshot.png`). That's the whole loop: `nav` →
48	`wait-for` the element you need → act (`click` / `fill` / `type` /
49	`press`) → `screenshot` → `console --errors` to check nothing threw.
50	Full command reference: `chromium-cli` skill, or `help` at the prompt.

58	import `{ chromium }` instead, launch with

32	```bash
33	chromium-cli --session app <<'EOF'
34	nav http://localhost:3000
35	wait-for text=Dashboard
36	screenshot
37	click button:has-text("New item")
38	fill input[name="title"] Smoke test
39	press Enter
40	wait-for text=Smoke test
41	screenshot
42	console --errors
43	EOF
44	```
45	
46	Screenshots land in `chromium_cli/sessions/app/screenshots/` (latest
47	symlinked as `screenshot.png`). That's the whole loop: `nav` →
48	`wait-for` the element you need → act (`click` / `fill` / `type` /
49	`press`) → `screenshot` → `console --errors` to check nothing threw.
50	Full command reference: `chromium-cli` skill, or `help` at the prompt.
51	
52	For iterative debugging, run it under tmux and `send-keys` one command
53	at a time — same commands, same session.
54	
55	**If `chromium-cli` isn't available:** adapt
56	[electron.md](electron.md)'s REPL driver — the structure and commands
57	transfer, but it's `_electron`-specific:
58	import `{ chromium }` instead, launch with
59	`chromium.launch({ args: ['--no-sandbox'] })`, acquire the page via
60	`(await app.newContext()).newPage()` then `goto()` your dev URL, and
61	drop the Electron-only window introspection
62	(`.windows()`/`.firstWindow()`/the `windows` command).
63	
64	## What to put in the skill
65	
66	The project-specific bits only. `chromium-cli` handles the mechanics.
67	
68	- **Dev command + port + stop.** The exact start line, any env vars it
69	  needs, and the `kill` to stop it.
70	- **Auth.** Whatever gets a logged-in session — a `set-cookie` line, a
71	  `fill`/`click` login sequence, or a helper script that does the API
72	  dance and emits the cookie.
73	- **One representative interaction.** Not the whole app — one path that
74	  proves it's running, ending in a screenshot.
75	- **App-specific gotchas.** Only the ones you actually hit.
76	
77	## Gotchas that recur
78	
79	- **React controlled inputs.** `eval el.value = '…'` doesn't fire
80	  React's onChange. Use `fill` / `type` — they go through Playwright's
81	  input pipeline.
82	- **Websockets / long-poll.** `wait-idle` never settles. `wait-for` the
83	  element you actually need.
84	- **Slow first paint.** Vite/Next compile routes on demand; the first
85	  `nav` can take 10s+. `wait-for` handles it; raw `sleep` doesn't.
86	- **`screenshot-element <sel>`** crops to one element — use it when the
87	  diff is in a specific component, not the whole page.
88	- **Check `console --errors` before declaring success.** A page can
89	  render its shell while every data fetch 500s.

## Summary

Added view transitions using React's `<ViewTransition>` component (bundled in Next.js 16's App Router canary React, no extra install needed — `next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/view-transitions.md` describes the exact API):

- **Shared-element morph**: `app/ProductGrid.tsx` and `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` wrap the thumbnail/hero image in matching `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="morph" default="none">`, so the browser morphs one image into the other across navigation.
- **Directional slides**: `app/nav-transition.ts` defines a shared `enter`/`exit` map keyed by `nav-forward`/`nav-back` transition types; grid links carry `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`, the back link carries `['nav-back']`, and both pages wrap their content in a `ViewTransition` using that map.
- **Suspense reveals**: the product page's fallback (`DetailsSkeleton`) is wrapped with `exit="slide-down"`, and the real content with `enter="slide-up"`, so the skeleton hands off to content instead of popping.
- **Reduced motion**: `app/globals.css` adds a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query that zeroes all view-transition animation durations/delays, plus `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` so clicks aren't swallowed mid-animation.
- Added `types/react-canary.d.ts` (`/// <reference types="react/canary" />`) so TypeScript recognizes the `ViewTransition` component's props.
